extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and practitioners concerned with the methodology of physical science, philosophy of science, and the relation between science and religion (scientists, philosophers, clergy, and informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance about the proper methodological boundary between physical science and theology/philosophy, and about what investigators may legitimately claim from physical inquiry. Advises on limits of scientific inference about moral, metaphysical, and human-personality questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science must be 'atheous' (take no account of God)
rubrics_metrics.description: All physical science, properly so called, is compelled by its very nature to take no account of the being of God: as soon as it does this, it trenches upon theology, and ceases to be physical science. If I might coin a word, I should say that science was atheous, and therefore could not be atheistic; that is to say, its investigations and reasonings are by agreement conversant simply with observed facts and conclusions drawn from them, and in this sense it is atheous, or without recognition of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation & example: A mathematician investigating clock mechanics or celestial mechanics treats the mechanism 'as it is' without considering the maker; this is not denial of the maker but a methodological exclusion. Scientists should not introduce theological considerations into physical inquiry; doing so removes the work from the province of physical science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a sacred 'scientific frontier' between science and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: We need a 'scientific frontier' between [God and nature], a line which shall on no condition be transgressed by those who occupy the territory on one side or the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale & warning: The frontier is not arbitrary but like a natural watershed; transgressing it tends to produce confusion and 'mischief.' Investigators should recognize and respect the boundary to avoid conflating physical description with metaphysical or moral claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not derive metaphysical or moral conclusions from purely physical investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: An investigator of nature has a right to say that the question of the existence of a beneficent Creator or the non-existence of such a Being does not affect his investigations; but he has no right, upon the strength of investigations purely physical, to deny the existence of beneficence as an attribute of the Creator, if a Creator there be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration & anti-pattern: The example of Ernst Haeckel shows how going beyond the scientific boundary led to a categorical denial of purpose and beneficence; scientists should avoid asserting atheistic moral conclusions on the basis of physical data alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: When treating anthropology as a physical science, confine scope to material attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: When anthropology is classed among the physical sciences, it is necessary to confine the investigations ... to the consideration of man as a creature having certain material attributes and leaving certain material marks of his existence in past ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitation note: Such a constrained anthropology is legitimate and of high interest, but it cannot be translated as 'the science of man' in the fullest sense because it leaves out moral, spiritual, and other non-material aspects of human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of scientific competence; avoid overreaching into philosophy or theology
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition and quality of mind which make a man a successful investigator of nature ... are seldom associated with those mental powers which enable a man to get beneath the surface of phenomena and speculate with any success as to the ground and underlying conditions of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: Scientists should be cautious about making broad metaphysical or philosophical claims beyond their expertise; while a mind may possess both kinds of power, the combination is rare and transgression of the frontier risks poor philosophy or mistaken conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep faith and science strictly apart in method and aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Where faith commences, science ends ... Faith has its origin in the poetic imagination; knowledge, on the other hand, originates in the reasoning intelligence of man. Science has to pluck the blessed fruits from the tree of knowledge, unconcerned whether these conquests trench upon the poetical imaginings of faith or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological prescription: Treat faith and scientific knowledge as distinct enterprises with different sources and methods; do not confuse poetic/theological claims with scientific explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious in proposing 'improvements' to natural arrangements; consider stability and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: It helps to illustrate the point ... the arrangement proposed by Laplace would not be stable — that is, that it would only be possible in the sense in which it is possible to make a pin stand upon its point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic caution: When suggesting changes to natural systems or asserting that nature could be 'improved,' ensure mathematical/physical stability and consider deeper constraints; superficial proposals may be impossible or unstable on analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that many human attributes (will, purpose, thought, personality) transcend physical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankind possess attributes which do not belong to other creatures ... the attribute of will, the attribute of purpose, the attribute of thought, and above all the attribute of personality — these seem not to be reducible simply to material conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research implication: Studies of such attributes require philosophical, moral, and religious lines of inquiry in addition to physical investigation; physical science alone will not yield a complete account of these aspects of human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material anomalies do not negate personal responsibility or identity
rubrics_metrics.description: What they [cases of double consciousness, insanity, idiocy] prove is, that we are dependent for the proper use of our faculties upon material conditions ... but they do not prove the unreality of the attribute of personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation guidance: In moral or legal judgment (e.g., witness credibility, responsibility), take account of material conditions and anomalies, but do not infer from them that personality or responsibility are unreal; context and full circumstances must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for an integrated ('scientific theism') view only by respecting distinct methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A really complete scientific theism ... would comprehend all the different departments ... and in the unity of such a system physicists and philosophers and divines would be able to meet and shake hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspirational note: While integration of physical, metaphysical, moral, and religious study is a desirable ideal, it requires respecting each branch's methods and sources; successful synthesis depends on not transgressing methodological boundaries recklessly.
